name: ML Privacy & Model Security
description: Privacy attacks against ML (membership inference, model/data extraction, inversion) and federated-learning security.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list, all from USENIX Security 2018, mark the moment when ML privacy and model security crystallized into a distinct research agenda. The work split along two lines that still organize the field. One line was defensive and protective: "AttriGuard: A Practical Defense Against Attribute Inference Attacks via Adversarial Machine Learning" (USENIX 2018) used adversarial perturbations to stop attackers from inferring users' hidden attributes, while "Turning Your Weakness Into a Strength: Watermarking Deep Neural Networks by Backdooring" (USENIX 2018) repurposed backdoors as a tool for claiming model ownership. The other line was offensive, exposing how much models leak: "With Great Training Comes Great Vulnerability: Practical Attacks against Transfer Learning" (USENIX 2018) showed that the now-common practice of fine-tuning shared backbones opens a clear attack surface, and "GAZELLE: A Low Latency Framework for Secure Neural Network Inference" (USENIX 2018) began the parallel effort to run inference without exposing data at all.

Around 2019-2020 the field grew more rigorous and more physical. "Evaluating Differentially Private Machine Learning in Practice" (USENIX 2019) pushed past theory to ask what a privacy budget really buys, becoming a reference point for honest accounting of DP defenses. At the same time, attackers moved off the math and onto the hardware: "CSI NN: Reverse Engineering of Neural Network Architectures Through Electromagnetic Side Channel" (USENIX 2019) and "Stealthy Tracking of Autonomous Vehicles with Cache Side Channels" (USENIX 2020) showed that side channels can steal architectures and track real systems. "Fawkes: Protecting Privacy against Unauthorized Deep Learning Models" (USENIX 2020) turned the protective instinct toward ordinary users, cloaking photos against facial recognition scrapers like Clearview.ai.

By 2022-2023 attention shifted decisively toward distributed training and generative models, and the volume of work exploded. Federated and split learning became a battleground: "FLAME: Taming Backdoors in Federated Learning" (USENIX 2022) defended the global model, while attacks like "VILLAIN: Backdoor Attacks Against Vertical Split Learning" (USENIX 2023) and "PCAT: Functionality and Data Stealing from Split Learning by Pseudo-Client Attack" (USENIX 2023) showed that splitting a model does not by itself protect the data inside it. Generative models brought their own crisis of memorization: "Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Models" (USENIX 2023), one of the most-cited papers here, demonstrated that image generators regurgitate their training data verbatim, and "CodexLeaks: Privacy Leaks from Code Generation Language Models in GitHub Copilot" (USENIX 2023) showed the same problem for code models in production.

Most recently the field has been responding to the dominance of large generative and foundation models on both the attack and defense sides. Defenses now aim to make generation itself private, as in "dp-promise: Differentially Private Diffusion Probabilistic Models for Image Synthesis" (USENIX 2024), and to harden deployed APIs against theft, as in "ModelGuard: Information-Theoretic Defense Against Model Extraction Attacks" (USENIX 2024). Cryptographic verifiability has matured from the inference frameworks of GAZELLE into scalable proofs, with "Scalable Zero-knowledge Proofs for Non-linear Functions in Machine Learning" (USENIX 2024). And the classic membership-inference question that animated the early work has been carried into the LLM era by "Towards Label-Only Membership Inference Attack against Pre-trained Large Language Models" (USENIX 2025), showing that even with only label access, one can probe what a large model has seen. The throughline across all these venues is a steady escalation: each new training paradigm and model class reopens the same privacy questions on harder terrain.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this NDSS thread staked out two problems that still anchor the field. On the integrity side, Trojaning Attack on Neural Networks (NDSS 2018) showed that the very act of sharing and adopting public models creates an opening to hide malicious behavior inside them. On the privacy side, Knock Knock, Who's There? Membership Inference on Aggregate Location Data (NDSS 2018) demonstrated that even coarse, aggregated data leaks who was in the training set, while De-anonymization of Mobility Trajectories (NDSS 2018) underscored how thin the line between anonymized and identifiable data really is.

Through 2020-2022 the attacks matured from proofs of concept into practical, optimized threats, and defenses arrived alongside them. CloudLeak (NDSS 2020) turned model stealing into a large-scale attack on commercial MLaaS using adversarial queries. Federated learning became a battleground: Manipulating the Byzantine (NDSS 2021), the most-cited FL paper in this set, formalized optimized model-poisoning attacks and defenses, and Data Poisoning Attacks to Deep Learning Based Recommender Systems (NDSS 2021) extended poisoning to deployed recommenders. Meanwhile membership inference grew more practical with Practical Blind Membership Inference Attack via Differential Comparisons (NDSS 2021), model inversion reached high-fidelity reconstruction in MIRROR (NDSS 2022), and defenses like DeepSight (NDSS 2022) began inspecting models to catch backdoors in federated settings.

By 2023-2024 the community was building infrastructure for privacy rather than only exposing leaks. Cryptographic and systems approaches matured through REDsec (NDSS 2023) for encrypted inference and Pencil (NDSS 2024) for collaborative learning without a non-colluding assumption, while attackers found new side channels such as Timing Channels in Adaptive Neural Networks (NDSS 2024). Federated defenses kept pace with Automatic Adversarial Adaption for Stealthy Poisoning Attacks (NDSS 2024) probing the limits of stealthy poisoning, and inversion defenses like Crafter (NDSS 2024) protected facial features at the edge.

The most recent work reflects two clear shifts: toward LLM serving and toward a defense-heavy federated agenda. I Know What You Asked (NDSS 2025) and its 2026 successor Shadow in the Cache: Unveiling and Mitigating Privacy Risks of KV-cache in LLM Inference moved the privacy frontier into multi-tenant LLM systems, where shared caches leak user prompts. Membership inference continued to sharpen with Cascading and Proxy Membership Inference Attacks (NDSS 2026), and rigorous privacy auditing surfaced in To Shuffle or not to Shuffle: Auditing DP-SGD with Shuffling (NDSS 2026). At the same time NDSS 2025-2026 is dominated by defenses — CENSOR and SVDefense against gradient inversion, SafeSplit against split-learning backdoors, WhiteCloak for accountable secure aggregation, and VeriLoRA using zero-knowledge proofs to make LLM fine-tuning verifiable — signaling a field that, having thoroughly mapped the attacks, is now consolidating around practical, provable protections for both federated training and large-model inference.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection treats a trained model as a target to be probed and pulled apart. Stealing Hyperparameters in Machine Learning (S&P 2018) showed that even the training recipe behind a model leaks through query access, and a year later Comprehensive Privacy Analysis of Deep Learning (S&P 2019) made the deeper point that models memorize their training data: it systematized membership inference across passive and active, white-box and black-box settings, and crucially extended it to federated learning. Exploiting Unintended Feature Leakage in Collaborative Learning (S&P 2019) drove the same message home for collaborative training, establishing early that sharing gradients is not the same as keeping data private.

Two responses ran in parallel. One was defensive cryptography and differential privacy: Differentially Private Model Publishing for Deep Learning and Towards Practical Differentially Private Convex Optimization (both S&P 2019), alongside secure-computation systems like Helen (S&P 2019), CrypTFlow (S&P 2020), and CryptGPU (S&P 2021), which pushed to make privacy-preserving training and inference practical. The other was a sharpening of the attacks themselves. Machine Unlearning (S&P 2021) reframed privacy as the right to have data removed from a model, while Adversary Instantiation (S&P 2021) probed how tight DP guarantees really are in practice.

The attacks then matured into a rigorous science. Membership Inference Attacks From First Principles (S&P 2022) rebuilt the field's evaluation methodology around low false-positive rates, exposing that many earlier attacks looked strong only under loose metrics. Reconstructing Training Data with Informed Adversaries (S&P 2022) raised the stakes from mere membership to recovering individual training records, and the threat surface widened to new model families — LINKTELLER and Model Stealing Attacks Against Inductive Graph Neural Networks (both S&P 2022) targeted graph models, DeepSteal (S&P 2022) stole weights through hardware side channels, and Property Inference from Poisoning (S&P 2022) fused inference with active tampering. Federated learning became its own battleground, with Back to the Drawing Board (S&P 2022) critically re-evaluating poisoning claims and defenses like FedRecover, RoFL, and ELSA (all S&P 2023) hardening aggregation against malicious clients.

The most recent work has decisively shifted toward large language models and toward closing the gap between formal guarantees and real leakage. Analyzing Leakage of Personally Identifiable Information in Language Models (S&P 2023) began quantifying how LLMs memorize personal data, and BOLT (S&P 2024) pushed private transformer inference. The 2026 papers show the frontier settling on federated LLMs and deployed model services: Toward Efficient Membership Inference Attacks Against Federated Large Language Models revisits membership inference for FedLLMs, ARES and On the Detectability of Active Gradient Inversion Attacks in Federated Learning renew the gradient-inversion arms race, and secure-inference systems like Euston target transformers directly. Most pointedly, Beyond Indistinguishability: Measuring Extraction Risk in LLM APIs (S&P 2026) argues that differential-privacy bounds and empirical membership tests understate the true extraction risk of production LLM APIs — a fitting bookend that returns to the field's founding worry, model memorization, now at the scale of language models served to millions.

ccs.narrative:
ML privacy research at CCS has dissected the information leakage surface of machine learning systems from multiple angles. The 2018 class introduced three foundational attack categories: Property Inference Attacks on Fully Connected Neural Networks using Permutation Invariant Representations (CCS 2018) extracted global training-set statistics, Machine Learning with Membership Privacy using Adversarial Regularization (CCS 2018) studied membership inference defenses, and Secure Outsourced Matrix Computation and Application to Neural Networks (CCS 2018) explored privacy-preserving inference via FHE.

The 2019-2020 period extended attacks to new model classes and sharpened defenses. MemGuard: Defending against Black-Box Membership Inference Attacks via Adversarial Examples (CCS 2019) added noise to confidence scores to protect membership status, while GAN-Leaks: A Taxonomy of Membership Inference Attacks against Generative Models (CCS 2020) and Information Leakage in Embedding Models (CCS 2020) broadened the threat beyond classifiers to generative and embedding models.

From 2022, federated learning became a central battleground. Enhanced Membership Inference Attacks against Machine Learning Models (CCS 2022) formalized attack evaluation as hypothesis testing, and Eluding Secure Aggregation in Federated Learning via Model Inconsistency (CCS 2022) showed that a malicious server can break secure aggregation. Truth Serum: Poisoning Machine Learning Models to Reveal Their Secrets (CCS 2022) revealed that poisoning amplifies privacy leakage, linking adversarial ML and ML privacy.

milestones.title: Property Inference Attacks on Fully Connected Neural Networks using Permutation Invariant Representations
milestones.note: Showed neural networks leak global dataset properties, establishing property inference as a distinct attack class.

milestones.title: Machine Learning with Membership Privacy using Adversarial Regularization
milestones.note: Proposed adversarial regularization as a training-time defense making models resistant to membership inference.

milestones.title: MemGuard: Defending against Black-Box Membership Inference Attacks via Adversarial Examples
milestones.note: Added carefully crafted noise to prediction confidence scores to deny membership inference attackers useful signals.

milestones.title: GAN-Leaks: A Taxonomy of Membership Inference Attacks against Generative Models
milestones.note: Systematized membership inference against GANs, expanding the threat beyond discriminative classifiers.

milestones.title: Information Leakage in Embedding Models
milestones.note: Demonstrated that text embedding models leak input attributes and can be inverted to recover sensitive data.

milestones.title: Enhanced Membership Inference Attacks against Machine Learning Models
milestones.note: Framed membership inference as hypothesis testing, producing stronger attacks that better audit training-data leakage.

milestones.title: Eluding Secure Aggregation in Federated Learning via Model Inconsistency
milestones.note: Broke federated learning's secure aggregation guarantee by exploiting model inconsistency on a malicious server.

milestones.title: Truth Serum: Poisoning Machine Learning Models to Reveal Their Secrets
milestones.note: Showed that data poisoning amplifies membership and attribute leakage, connecting adversarial and privacy ML threats.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work here split along two lines that the field has been braiding together ever since: attacks on the model itself and attacks on the data behind it. On the model-security side, "Trojaning Attack on Neural Networks" (NDSS 2018) showed that a shared, pre-trained network could be quietly implanted with a backdoor, and "Turning Your Weakness Into a Strength" (USENIX 2018) flipped that same backdooring trick into a watermark for proving ownership. On the privacy side, "Property Inference Attacks on Fully Connected Neural Networks" (CCS 2018) and "Stealing Hyperparameters in Machine Learning" (S&P 2018) demonstrated that even a model's aggregate properties and training recipe leak, while "Machine Learning with Membership Privacy using Adversarial Regularization" (CCS 2018) and "AttriGuard" (USENIX 2018) began building defenses. A parallel cryptographic thread — "GAZELLE" (USENIX 2018) and "Secure Outsourced Matrix Computation" (CCS 2018) — pursued the opposite goal of running inference without exposing data at all.

The 2019-2020 period sharpened the privacy attacks and pushed them into collaborative settings. "Comprehensive Privacy Analysis of Deep Learning" (S&P 2019) laid out passive and active white-box inference against both centralized and federated learning, and "Exploiting Unintended Feature Leakage in Collaborative Learning" (S&P 2019) showed that gradient sharing in federated training leaks far more than intended — a finding that later gradient-inversion work builds on directly. Differential privacy moved from theory to scrutiny with "Evaluating Differentially Private Machine Learning in Practice" (USENIX 2019) and "Differentially Private Model Publishing for Deep Learning" (S&P 2019). Attacks then broadened past classifiers: "GAN-Leaks" (CCS 2020) built a taxonomy of membership inference against generative models, "Information Leakage in Embedding Models" (CCS 2020) and "Privacy Risks of General-Purpose Language Models" (S&P 2020) targeted representations and early language models, and "Fawkes" (USENIX 2020) turned privacy attacks around into a user-side cloaking tool.

By 2021-2023 the area matured into rigor, new problem framings, and adversarial contests. "Machine Unlearning" (S&P 2021) formalized data deletion, and "When Machine Unlearning Jeopardizes Privacy" (CCS 2021) immediately showed the deletion operation itself can leak. Federated learning became a security battleground: "Manipulating the Byzantine" (NDSS 2021) optimized model-poisoning attacks and defenses, "FLAME" (USENIX 2022) tamed backdoors, and "Back to the Drawing Board" (S&P 2022) critically questioned whether these poisoning threats hold up on production FL. Membership inference was put on firmer footing by "Membership Inference Attacks From First Principles" (S&P 2022) and "Enhanced Membership Inference Attacks against Machine Learning Models" (CCS 2022), which insisted on low-false-positive evaluation. Attention then shifted to large generative and language models, with "Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Models" (USENIX 2023) proving verbatim memorization and "Analyzing Leakage of Personally Identifiable Information in Language Models" (S&P 2023) measuring real PII exposure.

The most recent work (NDSS 2026) reflects a field now organized around LLMs, tighter auditing, and accountable federated infrastructure. Membership inference keeps advancing with "Cascading and Proxy Membership Inference Attacks" and "In-Context Probing for Membership Inference in Fine-Tuned Language Models," while "Shadow in the Cache" exposes a genuinely new surface — privacy leakage from the KV-cache during LLM inference. Differential privacy has turned inward on its own guarantees in "To Shuffle or not to Shuffle: Auditing DP-SGD with Shuffling" and produced deployable artifacts like "PrivORL" for offline RL. Federated and outsourced learning now emphasize verifiable, malicious-secure protocols — "SVDefense" against gradient inversion, "WhiteCloak" for holding anonymous clients accountable in secure aggregation, "CRISP" against malicious clients, and "VeriLoRA" using zero-knowledge proofs for verifiable fine-tuning — showing the area moving from demonstrating leakage toward provable, accountable defenses.
